_about: GENERATED by tools/periods-from-vault.py from CWVault/claude/Periods-Deep-*.md — do not edit by hand; edit the markdown and run the tool. The words of the periods of stories/deep-time.json, keyed by name: the summary (its trailing More removed; the page adds the word), the More as paragraphs with its span line, the official name, known from, what opens and what is inside, the references, the Pictures wanted line as data, and the Checked line. The tree carries the period's edges and colour; where the words' Span differs the tree wins on the page. Read by active/time-machine.html.

Molten.name: Molten
Molten.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries, rounded: the chart has 4,567 (the oldest grains in meteorites, ratified 2022) and 4,031 ± 3 (the oldest rock, Acasta, since 2023)
Molten.officialName: Hadean, after Hades, the Greek god of the dead and the underworld he ruled; named by Preston Cloud in 1972
Molten.knownFrom: a few zircon crystals, smaller than grains of sand, and some moon rocks and meteorites
Molten.insideIt: events *Oldest grains*, *Gathering*, *Moon formed*, *Black Earth*, *Blue Earth*, *Grey Earth* (at the end edge). Plots: *Day length* and *Sun and inside* begin at *Moon formed*; *Minerals* and *Continents* begin at 4,567.
Molten.picturesWanted: a painting of the magma ocean with the close Moon (NASA or ESA artwork; licence to check); a Jack Hills zircon in cathodoluminescence (John Valley, University of Wisconsin; licence to ask).
Molten.summary: The whole surface of the Earth was melted rock, under a sky of steam. Within a few million years it froze over, the steam rained down, and there was a sea. The Moon was new.

more.spanLine: From about 4.6 to 4 billion years ago.
paragraphs: At the start of this stretch there was nowhere to stand. The whole surface of the Earth was melted rock, glowing, and perhaps hundreds of kilometres deep. Above it hung air made of rock vapour and steam. The Earth had just been hit by another young planet, and the Moon had formed from the wreck (*Moon formed*). Through a gap in the steam, the Moon would probably have looked about twenty times wider than it does now, because it was that much closer.

The name *Molten* fits only the beginning. Models say the surface froze over within a few million years. Then the steam rained out, and the Earth had a sea. At first the sea was far hotter than boiling water. It stayed liquid because the thick air above it pressed down so hard.

By 4.4 billion years ago there was probably cool water at the surface. A crystal that formed then still remembers it (*Blue Earth*). So for nearly all of these 600 million years the Earth had a solid crust and a sea, and rocks from space kept falling on both.
What is new in this stretch is the planet itself: the Earth, with its Moon, then a crust, then a sea.

Almost nothing from it survives. There is no rock from most of it, only tiny crystals of zircon, a mineral so hard that it outlasts the rock it grew in. The oldest rock that nearly every geologist accepts formed beside the Acasta River in northern Canada, about 4.03 billion years ago (*Grey Earth*). That rock marks the end of this stretch.
Six hundred million years is about an eighth of the Earth's whole life. It is nearly as long as the whole Animals line, from the first animals to now.
Geologists call this stretch the Hadean ("hay-DEE-un"), after Hades, the Greek god of the dead and the underworld he ruled. Preston Cloud, an American geologist, gave it the name in 1972.
Whether anything was alive in it, nobody knows.

references: Kevin Zahnle and others, "Emergence of a habitable planet," *Space Science Reviews*, 2007. The magma ocean freezing, the steam raining out, the hot sea under heavy air, the close Moon.

Simon Wilde, John Valley, William Peck and Colin Graham, "Evidence from detrital zircons for the existence of continental crust and oceans on the Earth 4.4 Gyr ago," *Nature*, 2001. Water by 4.4 billion.
Jaana Halla and others, "Ratification of the base of the ICS Geological Time Scale: the GSSA for the Hadean lower boundary," *Episodes*, 2024. The official start.
Robert Hazen, *The Story of Earth* (Viking, 2012). For a parent.

Oceans.name: Oceans
Oceans.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries: 4,000 is our rounding of the chart's 4,031 ± 3; 2,500 is a boundary fixed by agreement (1990), not by a layer of rock
Oceans.officialName: Archean, from the Greek for "ancient", which comes from the word for "beginning"; named by James Dwight Dana in 1872
Oceans.knownFrom: the oldest surviving rock, from about 4 billion years ago, and mounds built by microbes, from about 3.4 billion
Oceans.insideIt: events *Grey Earth* (at the start edge), *Bombardment*, *Stromatolites*, *Kenorland*, *Cyanobacteria* (at the end edge). Plots: *Oxygen* (begins at 4,000, near nothing), *Continents* (land a few hundredths of the surface), *Sun and inside*, *Day length*, *Minerals*.
Oceans.picturesWanted: the stromatolites at Strelley Pool, Pilbara (Geological Survey of Western Australia or Commons; licence to check); living stromatolites at Hamelin Pool, Shark Bay, as a picture of what the mounds were like (Commons; licence to check).
Oceans.summary: A world of sea, with a few low islands and almost no other dry land. There was no oxygen in the air. In shallow water, microbes built mounds, the oldest life we can point to.

more.spanLine: From about 4 to 2.5 billion years ago.
paragraphs: In the Pilbara of Western Australia, near a waterhole called Strelley Pool, there is rock that was once the floor of a shallow sea. In it are low mounds and cones, row on row for kilometres. Microbes built them about 3.4 billion years ago, layer on layer, as living mats trapped sand and grew up through it (*Stromatolites*).

Stand on that sea floor and almost everything around is water. For most of this stretch there was very little dry land, mainly volcanic islands. By some estimates, even near its end only two or three parts in a hundred of the Earth's surface stood above the sea. Today it is about thirty.
The air held no oxygen to breathe. Nobody knows the colour of the sky. Near the end, a haze may have come and gone, each time for less than a million years.

The Sun was about a fifth dimmer than now, yet the sea did not freeze. Why not is still argued. The days were short: tidal layers in South Africa suggest about thirteen hours, about 3.2 billion years ago.

What is new in this stretch is rock that survives, and life we can point to. Before it there are only crystals; from it there are whole mountainsides. And in its rocks are the oldest signs of life that most geologists accept.

All of that life was microbes, each too small to see. Near the end, some of them were probably already using sunlight to split water and give off oxygen, but almost none of the oxygen reached the air (*Cyanobacteria*).
A billion and a half years is a third of the Earth's whole life. It is about twice as long as the Animals line.

Geologists call this stretch the Archean ("ar-KEE-un"), from the Greek word for "ancient", which comes from the word for "beginning". James Dwight Dana, an American geologist, gave it the name in 1872.

references: Abigail Allwood, Malcolm Walter, Balz Kamber, Craig Marshall and Ian Burch, "Stromatolite reef from the Early Archaean era of Australia," *Nature*, 2006. The scene.

Nicolas Flament, Nicolas Coltice and Patrice Rey, "A case for late-Archaean continental emergence from thermal evolution models and hypsometry," *Earth and Planetary Science Letters*, 2008. How little land there was.
Aubrey Zerkle and others, "A bistable organic-rich atmosphere on the Neoarchaean Earth," *Nature Geoscience*, 2012. The haze that came and went.
Andrew Knoll, *A Brief History of Earth* (Custom House, 2021). For a parent.

Oxygen.name: Oxygen
Oxygen.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries fixed by agreement (1990), not by layers of rock
Oxygen.officialName: the first part of the Proterozoic, "earlier life" (from Greek *proteros*, earlier, and *zoe*, life), named by Samuel Franklin Emmons in the late 1880s; geologists split this part into the Siderian, Rhyacian and Orosirian, from Greek words for iron, a stream of lava and a range of mountains
Oxygen.knownFrom: rock that records the air: red soils and sandstones, banded iron, and sulphur in shale
Oxygen.insideIt: events *Short days*, *Great freeze*, *Oxygen in the air*, *Red rocks*, *Banded iron*, *Nuna* (at the end edge). Plots: *Oxygen* (the rise at about 2,430 and the coming and going to about 2,220), *Day length* (about 17 hours at 2,460), *Minerals*.
Oxygen.picturesWanted: the banded iron walls of Joffre Gorge or Dales Gorge, Karijini (Commons or Parks and Wildlife WA; licence to check); a polished slab of banded iron (Commons; licence to check).
Oxygen.summary: Stripes of iron were settling on the sea floor, and ice came and went. Then, for the first time, oxygen stayed in the air. There was only a little, but it turned the ground red.

more.spanLine: From about 2.5 to 1.8 billion years ago.
paragraphs: In Karijini, in the Pilbara of Western Australia, the walls of Joffre Gorge are striped. Red bands rich in iron lie between grey and black ones, thousands of them, each laid down on the floor of a sea about two and a half billion years ago (*Banded iron*). The stripes keep time. Read as a record of the Moon's pull, they say that a day then lasted about seventeen hours (*Short days*).

At the start of this stretch the air still held almost no oxygen. Then, about 2.43 billion years ago, the oxygen made by microbes in the sea began to stay in the air (*Oxygen in the air*). It did not stay at once. For about two hundred million years it came and went, and only by about 2.2 billion years ago was it there for good.
That is what is new: oxygen in the air, for the first time.

There was never much of it in this stretch. How much is argued: at its highest, perhaps a few parts in a hundred of today's, and probably far less near the end. But a little was enough to change the ground. Iron in rock rusts when oxygen reaches it, and soils and sand began to turn red (*Red rocks*). Many minerals that need oxygen to form could form for the first time.

The oxygen may also have brought the cold. Methane, a gas that kept the Earth warm, is destroyed by oxygen. Ice spread several times in this stretch, as far as land that lay near the equator (*Great freeze*).
All the life was still microbes. The deep sea still had no oxygen at all.
Seven hundred million years is about as long as the whole Animals line, from the first animals to now.
Geologists call this stretch the first part of the Proterozoic ("pro-ter-o-ZOH-ik"), Greek for "earlier life". Its three parts have names that mean iron, a stream of lava and a range of mountains.
Near its end, most of the land may have come together into one great continent (*Nuna*).

references: Simon Poulton and others, "A 200-million-year delay in permanent atmospheric oxygenation," *Nature*, 2021. Oxygen coming and going, and staying from about 2.22 billion.
Ashley Gumsley and others, "Timing and tempo of the Great Oxidation Event," *PNAS*, 2017. The first rise and the first ice.
Timothy Lyons, Christopher Reinhard and Noah Planavsky, "The rise of oxygen in Earth's early ocean and atmosphere," *Nature*, 2014. How much, and how sure.
Nick Lane, *Oxygen: The Molecule That Made the World* (Oxford University Press, 2002). For a parent.

Big cells.name: Big cells
Big cells.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries fixed by agreement, not by layers of rock (1,800 since 1990; 720 provisional, pending a point in the rock, perhaps at the start of the first snowball, about 717)
Big cells.officialName: no single name: the end of the Paleoproterozoic, the whole Mesoproterozoic, and the Tonian (the middle of the Proterozoic, "earlier life"); some geologists call it the boring billion
Big cells.knownFrom: fossils of single cells and ribbons in shale, mounds built by microbes, and chemistry in the rock
Big cells.insideIt: events *Nuna* (at the start edge), *Cells with nuclei*, *Bangiomorpha*, *Rodinia cracks*. Plots: *Oxygen* (low and flat), *Day length*, *Minerals*.
Big cells.picturesWanted: the ribbon fossils of the Gaoyuzhuang Formation, Hebei (Zhu and others 2016, *Nature Communications*, open access, CC BY; to confirm); *Bangiomorpha* under the microscope (Nicholas Butterfield; licence to ask).
Big cells.summary: A quiet sea for a billion years, with little oxygen and no ice. In it lived a new kind of cell, bigger than a bacterium, with a nucleus. Some stuck together, and grew long.

more.spanLine: From about 1.8 billion to 720 million years ago.
paragraphs: In the hills of Hebei, in northern China, there is shale that was mud on the floor of a shallow sea about 1.56 billion years ago. Split it open and some layers hold dark ribbons, a few of them as long as a school ruler. Each ribbon was a living thing made of many cells, probably using sunlight like seaweed.

A sea like that would have looked calm. There were no plants on land, no animals, and no ice anywhere. The air held a little oxygen, how much is argued, and the deep water held none. In places the water stank of rotten eggs. The Moon was closer than now, and a day lasted about eighteen or nineteen hours.

For a long time this stretch seemed so steady that three geologists wrote, in 1995, that never in the Earth's history "did so little happen to so much for so long". It has been called the boring billion. That may be unfair. Oxygen seems to have risen and fallen in pulses, and the continents came together into one (*Nuna*), broke apart, and came together again into another, called Rodinia, which began to crack near the end (*Rodinia cracks*).

What is new is the cell with a nucleus: a cell that keeps its genes in a small bag of their own. Such cells are often ten times as wide as bacteria, and they are the kind that every plant, animal and fungus is made of. The oldest fossils of them that most scientists accept are about 1.65 billion years old (*Cells with nuclei*). About 1.05 billion years ago a red seaweed on what is now Somerset Island, in Nunavut, left the oldest evidence of sex (*Bangiomorpha*).
A billion years and more is nearly a quarter of the Earth's whole life. It is one and a half times as long as the Animals line.
Geologists have no single name for it. It is the middle of the Proterozoic, "earlier life".
Just after it ended, ice spread from the poles almost to the equator (*Snowball one*).

references: Maoyan Zhu and others, "Decimetre-scale multicellular eukaryotes from the 1.56-billion-year-old Gaoyuzhuang Formation in North China," *Nature Communications*, 2016. The scene.

Roger Buick, David Des Marais and Andrew Knoll, "Stable isotopic compositions of carbonates from the Mesoproterozoic Bangemall Group, northwestern Australia," *Chemical Geology*, 1995. "So little… for so long".
Timothy Gibson and others, "Precise age of *Bangiomorpha pubescens* dates the origin of eukaryotic photosynthesis," *Geology*, 2018.
Andrew Knoll, *Life on a Young Planet* (Princeton University Press, 2003). For a parent.

Animals.name: Animals
Animals.spanNote: the start a dated boundary fixed by agreement (the start of the Cryogenian, provisional); moved from a guessed 700 on 10 Oct
Animals.officialName: none for the whole; it starts about 180 million years before the Phanerozoic, Greek for "visible life", which begins 539 million years ago (named by George Chadwick in 1930)
Animals.knownFrom: fossils of animals with hard parts, from about 539 million years ago; before that, rare soft fossils and argued chemistry
Animals.insideIt: every event from *Snowball one* (717) to now, about sixty. By line: Soft bodies, ten; Trilobites, twelve; Dinosaurs, six; Mammals, ten, and the twelve of batch 6. Plots: *Sea level* (from 540), *Oxygen*, *People* (from 315,000 years ago).
Animals.index: the horse and the elephant line, followed down the Mammals line as events (batch 3)
Animals.picturesWanted: a living sponge, as the animal the oldest argued chemistry points to (Commons; licence to check); a blue whale beside a frond from Mistaken Point, drawn to one scale (to make).
Animals.summary: The first animals were probably small and soft, and left almost nothing behind. Then they grew, a millionfold in a hundred and fifty million years: fronds, trilobites, fish, dinosaurs, whales.

more.spanLine: From about 720 million years ago to now.
paragraphs: At the start of this stretch, ice was about to spread over almost the whole Earth (*Snowball one*). Somewhere in the sea there were probably animals already. Nobody has found them. They were probably small and soft, and they left almost nothing behind.

How can anyone say they were there? From their descendants. Every living animal carries genes copied from its parents, with small changes each time. Counting the differences between the genes of living animals, and how fast such changes pile up, gives a rough date for their common ancestor. The answers run from about 800 to 650 million years ago. In older rock in Oman there is also a chemical that some scientists read as made by sponges, the simplest animals. Others think algae made it. That is still argued.
What is new is animals: living things made of many cells that eat other living things. Most of them move.

Then they grew. The oldest big fossils that may be animals are about 574 million years old: fronds and quilted shapes on the sea floor, some nearly two metres long (*Mistaken Point*). From about 600 to 450 million years ago the biggest living things became about a million times bigger. Then came trilobites, fish, trees, dinosaurs, and today the blue whale, the heaviest animal known.

The four stretches below are named for what was most noticed in each, not for what arrived first. There were no trilobites at the start of Trilobites, and no dinosaurs at the start of Dinosaurs. Mammals had already lived for about a hundred and forty million years when Mammals began.
Seven hundred and twenty million years is about a sixth of the Earth's whole life.

Geologists have no single name for it. Their Phanerozoic ("fan-er-o-ZOH-ik"), Greek for "visible life", starts later, about 539 million years ago, where fossils of animals with hard parts begin to fill the rocks (*Animals, kept*).
When the first animal lived, and what it looked like, nobody knows.

references: Mario dos Reis and others, "Uncertainty in the timing of origin of animals and the limits of precision in molecular timescales," *Current Biology*, 2015. The gene clocks.
Jonathan Payne and others, "Two-phase increase in the maximum size of life over 3.5 billion years," *PNAS*, 2009. The millionfold growth.
Douglas Erwin and others, "The Cambrian conundrum: early divergence and later ecological success in the early history of animals," *Science*, 2011. Animals older than their fossils.
Richard Fortey, *Life: An Unauthorised Biography* (HarperCollins, 1997). For a parent.

Soft bodies.name: Soft bodies
Soft bodies.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries: 720 fixed by agreement (provisional); 539 a point in the rock at Fortune Head, Newfoundland, dated 538.8 ± 0.6
Soft bodies.officialName: Cryogenian, "birth of ice", and Ediacaran, after the Ediacara Hills of South Australia, an Aboriginal name whose meaning is argued
Soft bodies.knownFrom: glacial rubble at the equator, and impressions of soft bodies in sandstone and volcanic ash
Soft bodies.insideIt: events *Snowball one*, *Snowball two*, *The thaw*, *Little balls*, *Gaskiers*, *Mistaken Point*, *Charnia*, *Dickinsonia*, *Bites and shells*, *Animals, kept* (at the end edge). Plots: *Oxygen*, *Day length* (about 22 hours at 620).
Soft bodies.picturesWanted: the fronds on the E Surface at Mistaken Point (UNESCO or Parks and Natural Areas, Newfoundland and Labrador; licence to check); a *Dickinsonia* fossil (Commons; licence to check).
Soft bodies.summary: Ice covered nearly the whole Earth, twice. When it melted, big soft things grew on the sea floor: fronds, quilts, discs. Some were animals. None had a shell or a mouth that bit, until the end.

more.spanLine: From about 720 to 539 million years ago.
paragraphs: At Mistaken Point, on the southern tip of Newfoundland, the sea has worn the cliffs down to flat sheets of grey rock. On them lie thousands of fossils: fronds like feathers, branched like ferns, some a hand long and some nearly two metres. About 565 million years ago they stood up from the mud of a deep sea floor, where sunlight probably did not reach. Then ash from a volcano settled over them and kept them where they stood (*Mistaken Point*).
Nothing in that scene could bite. None of the fronds had a mouth. Many of them may have fed by soaking up food from the water through their skin.

That is what is new: big living things with soft bodies, the oldest large fossils there are. Some, like *Dickinsonia*, an oval quilt up to more than a metre long, were animals: its fossils still hold a fat that only animals make (*Dickinsonia*). What many of the others were, nobody knows.

The stretch began in ice. Twice, ice spread from the poles almost to the equator, first for about fifty-seven million years (*Snowball one*), then for a few million (*Snowball two*). For about a third of this stretch the Earth was white. When the second ice melted, it melted fast (*The thaw*).

Near the end, the soft world began to change. About 550 million years ago, small animals in Namibia built tubes of shell, and some of the tubes have neat holes drilled in them, the oldest known bites (*Bites and shells*).
A hundred and eighty million years is a quarter of the Animals line. It is nearly three times as long as everything since the dinosaurs died.

Geologists split this stretch in two. The Cryogenian ("cry-o-JEN-ee-un"), "birth of ice", is the time of the two snowballs. The Ediacaran ("ee-dee-AK-a-run") is named after the Ediacara Hills in South Australia. It was added in 2004, the first new period in more than a hundred years.
At its end, animals with hard parts begin to fill the rocks (*Animals, kept*).

references: Jack Matthews and others, "A chronostratigraphic framework for the rise of the Ediacaran macrobiota: new constraints from Mistaken Point Ecological Reserve, Newfoundland," *GSA Bulletin*, 2021. The scene and its dates.
Andrew Knoll, Malcolm Walter, Guy Narbonne and Nicholas Christie-Blick, "The Ediacaran Period: a new addition to the geologic time scale," *Lethaia*, 2006. The name and its date.
Paul Hoffman and others, "Snowball Earth climate dynamics and Cryogenian geology-geobiology," *Science Advances*, 2017. The two ices.
Mark McMenamin, *The Garden of Ediacara* (Columbia University Press, 1998). For a parent.

Trilobites.name: Trilobites
Trilobites.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 538.8 ± 0.6 (Fortune Head, Newfoundland) and 251.902 ± 0.024 (Meishan, Zhejiang)
Trilobites.officialName: Paleozoic, "ancient life"; Adam Sedgwick's word (1838), stretched to this whole span by John Phillips in 1840
Trilobites.knownFrom: fossils of animals and plants with hard parts, in rock laid down in seas, swamps and rivers
Trilobites.opensTo: Shells, Crowded seas, Green land, Fish, Coal forests, One continent
Trilobites.insideIt: events *Animals, kept* (at the start edge), *Chengjiang*, *Burgess Shale*, *The map clears*, *Plants ashore*, *Short, sharp ice*, *Jaws*, *Animals ashore*, *Forests*, *Tiktaalik*, *Land egg*, *Coal*, *The Great Dying* (at the end edge). Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen* (the high near 300).
Trilobites.picturesWanted: a trilobite from Chengjiang, legs and all (Yunnan Key Laboratory for Palaeobiology or Commons; licence to check); a trilobite eye, its lenses visible (Commons; licence to check).
Trilobites.summary: The seas filled with animals that had shells, legs and eyes, and the commonest were trilobites. Then plants and animals came onto the land, and forests grew. At the end, nearly everything died.

more.spanLine: From about 539 to 252 million years ago.
paragraphs: At Chengjiang, in Yunnan, in southern China, there is shale that was mud on the floor of a shallow sea about 518 million years ago. Mud slid over the animals living there and buried them so quickly that their soft parts were kept: legs, guts, eyes. Nearly two hundred kinds of animal have been found in it (*Chengjiang*). Many crawled on the sea floor. Some swam above it. Some had claws for catching the others.

The commonest fossils there, as in rocks of this age all over the world, are trilobites ("TRY-lo-bites"). A trilobite was an armoured animal with many jointed legs. Most were about the size of a finger; the biggest known was longer than a child's arm. Their eyes had lenses made of a clear mineral, calcite, which turned to stone with the rest of them, so they are among the oldest eyes that can be studied lens by lens. More than twenty thousand kinds have been named.
Yet there were no trilobites at the start of this stretch. The oldest found are about 521 million years old, so for the first eighteen million years there were none to find.

What is new is a world of hard parts: shells, spines, jaws, eyes. And, in the middle of the stretch, the land turned green. Plants came ashore (*Plants ashore*), then small animals (*Animals ashore*), then forests (*Forests*), then animals with four legs (*Tiktaalik*), and then eggs that could be laid on dry land (*Land egg*).
Trilobites were most various about 470 million years ago. After that they dwindled. By the end there were only a few kinds left, small ones.
Two hundred and ninety million years is two fifths of the Animals line. It is longer than the Dinosaurs line and the Mammals line put together.
Geologists call this stretch the Paleozoic ("pay-lee-o-ZOH-ik"), "ancient life". Adam Sedgwick, an English geologist, made the word in 1838, and John Phillips stretched it to this whole span in 1840.
The last trilobites died in the Great Dying, with four in five kinds of sea animal (*The Great Dying*).

references: John Paterson, Gregory Edgecombe and Michael Lee, "Trilobite evolutionary rates constrain the duration of the Cambrian explosion," *PNAS*, 2019. The oldest trilobites.
Brigitte Schoenemann, Helje Pärnaste and Euan Clarkson, "Structure and function of a compound eye, more than half a billion years old," *PNAS*, 2017. The eyes.
Richard Fortey, *Trilobite! Eyewitness to Evolution* (HarperCollins, 2000). For a parent.

Dinosaurs.name: Dinosaurs
Dinosaurs.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 251.902 ± 0.024 (Meishan, Zhejiang) and 66.0 (El Kef, Tunisia)
Dinosaurs.officialName: Mesozoic, "middle life"; named by John Phillips in 1840
Dinosaurs.knownFrom: fossils in rock laid down on land and in shallow seas, and the seafloor's magnetic stripes from about 200 million years ago
Dinosaurs.insideIt: events *The Great Dying* (at the start edge), *Lystrosaurus* (new, below), *Dinosaurs*, *Pangaea cracks*, *Triassic ends*, *Archaeopteryx*, *Oldest flowers*, *The asteroid* (at the end edge). Plots: *Sea level* (high in the Cretaceous), *Oxygen*.
Dinosaurs.picturesWanted: a *Lystrosaurus* skeleton (Iziko South African Museum or Commons; licence to check); a map of Pangaea at 250 million years (our own map, at that year).
Dinosaurs.summary: The Great Dying left one continent, hot and nearly empty. For millions of years it filled slowly. Dinosaurs arrived about twenty million years in, and ruled the land for most of the rest.

more.spanLine: From about 252 to 66 million years ago.
paragraphs: In the Karoo of South Africa, a dry country of flat-topped hills, there are layers of old river mud from just after the Great Dying. Nine in ten of the bones found in them belong to one animal: *Lystrosaurus* ("liss-tro-SAW-rus"), a stocky plant-eater about a metre long, with two tusks and a beak (*Lystrosaurus*).

That emptiness is the scene. All the land was joined in one continent, Pangaea, and much of its middle was desert. In the tropics the sea at the surface may have been as hot as a hot bath, about 40 °C, and for about five million years almost no fish or reptiles lived there. It took eight or nine million years for the living world to fill up again.

There were no dinosaurs in it. The oldest found, in Brazil and Argentina, are about 233 to 231 million years old, nearly twenty million years after this stretch began (*Dinosaurs*). Even then they were not in charge. For a long time the reptiles on the crocodile side of the family were more common and came in more shapes.

Then, about 201 million years ago, Pangaea began to crack open, volcanoes poured out lava along the cracks, and another dying took away many of those rivals (*Pangaea cracks*, *Triassic ends*). After it, dinosaurs ruled the land.

What is new is the dinosaurs, and the world they lived in: for most of this stretch the Earth was warm, with little or no ice at the poles. Birds appeared (*Archaeopteryx*), and so did flowers (*Oldest flowers*). Small mammals lived through most of it.
A hundred and eighty-six million years is a quarter of the Animals line. It is nearly three times as long as the Mammals line.
Geologists call this stretch the Mesozoic ("mez-o-ZOH-ik"), "middle life". John Phillips, an English geologist, gave it the name in 1840.
It ended about 66 million years ago, when an asteroid about ten kilometres across hit what is now Yucatán, in Mexico, and every dinosaur died except the birds (*The asteroid*).

references: Zhong-Qiang Chen and Michael Benton, "The timing and pattern of biotic recovery following the end-Permian mass extinction," *Nature Geoscience*, 2012. Eight or nine million years.
Yadong Sun and others, "Lethally hot temperatures during the Early Triassic greenhouse," *Science*, 2012. The hot tropics.
Stephen Brusatte, Michael Benton, Marcello Ruta and Graeme Lloyd, "Superiority, competition, and opportunism in the evolutionary radiation of dinosaurs," *Science*, 2008. The crocodile line first.
Stephen Brusatte, *The Rise and Fall of the Dinosaurs* (William Morrow, 2018). For a parent.

Mammals.name: Mammals
Mammals.spanNote: the start a dated boundary at a point in the rock: 66.0 (El Kef, Tunisia)
Mammals.officialName: Cenozoic, "new life"; named by John Phillips in 1840
Mammals.knownFrom: fossils, seafloor mud cored by drilling ships, and, at the end, ice cores
Mammals.insideIt: events *The asteroid* (at the start edge), *Fern spike* (new, below), *Hot spike*, *Antarctica freezes*, *Grasslands*, *Hot-country grasses*, *Walking upright*, *Stone tools*, *Panama closes*, *Ice by turns*, *Homo sapiens*, *Last glacial maximum*, and the twelve of batch 6 (*Shell beads* to *Altamira*). Plots: *Sea level*, *People* (from 315,000 years ago).
Mammals.index: the horse (cat-sized at the start of *Heat*) and the elephant line, followed down the lines as events (batch 3)
Mammals.picturesWanted: the cliffs at Corral Bluffs, Colorado (Denver Museum of Nature and Science; licence to ask); a fossil palm leaf from the first hundred thousand years (the same).
Mammals.summary: After the asteroid, ferns covered the burnt land, and the biggest mammals left were the size of rats. Within a million years some were the size of wolves. Mammals were old; being big was new.

more.spanLine: From about 66 million years ago to now.
paragraphs: At Corral Bluffs, in Colorado, the rock holds the first million years after the asteroid, layer on layer. Just above the layer of the impact, nearly all the fossil pollen is from ferns (*Fern spike*). The biggest mammals that lived through the impact there weighed about half a kilogram, the size of a rat. Within about a hundred thousand years there were palm forests, and mammals the size of raccoons. Within about three hundred thousand, some weighed as much as a big dog. By seven hundred thousand years there were beans, and mammals the size of wolves.
That is what is new: mammals got big.

Mammals themselves were old. The oldest ones known, small animals like shrews, lived about 140 million years before this stretch began. Through the whole age of dinosaurs most mammals stayed small. So mammals had lived more than twice as long before this stretch as they have lived in it.

Later in the stretch, the Earth went through a sudden heat (*Hot spike*), then a long cooling, with ice settling on Antarctica (*Antarctica freezes*). Grass spread over the plains (*Grasslands*), and near the end, ice came and went across the north again and again (*Ice by turns*).
Sixty-six million years is about a tenth of the Animals line. Trilobites lasted more than four times as long.
Geologists call this stretch the Cenozoic ("see-no-ZOH-ik"), "new life". John Phillips, an English geologist, gave it the name in 1840.
The name marks the animals that grew large on land. It does not mean the dinosaurs had gone. Birds are dinosaurs, and there are more kinds of bird alive today than of mammal.

references: Tyler Lyson and others, "Exceptional continental record of biotic recovery after the Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction," *Science*, 2019. The scene.
Robert Tschudy and others, "Disruption of the terrestrial plant ecosystem at the Cretaceous-Tertiary boundary, Western Interior," *Science*, 1984. The ferns.
Stephen Brusatte, *The Rise and Reign of the Mammals* (Mariner Books, 2022). For a parent.

Shells.name: Shells
Shells.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 538.8 ± 0.6 (Fortune Head, Newfoundland) and 486.85 ± 1.5 (Green Point, Newfoundland); 487 replaces 485 (Michael, 10 Oct), because 485 lay outside the chart's error
Shells.officialName: Cambrian, from Cambria, the name for Wales in medieval Latin, itself from *Cymry*, the Welsh people's name for themselves; named by Adam Sedgwick in 1835
Shells.knownFrom: shells, trilobites and burrows in sea rock all over the world, and a few beds of mud that kept soft bodies too
Shells.insideIt: events *Animals, kept* (at the start edge), *Chengjiang*, *Burgess Shale*, *The map clears*. Plots: *Sea level* (begins at 540), *Oxygen*.
Shells.picturesWanted: archaeocyath limestone at the Ajax Mine reef or Wilkawillina Gorge (Geological Survey of South Australia or Commons; licence to check); a single archaeocyath cup in section (Commons; licence to check).
Shells.summary: The seas filled with animals that had hard parts (shells, spines, armour) and eyes. Within twenty million years, most great branches of the animal family turned up. Sponge-like animals and lime-making microbes built some of the first big reefs.

more.spanLine: From about 539 to 487 million years ago.
paragraphs: In the Flinders Ranges of South Australia, near an old mine called Ajax, there is grey limestone that was once a reef in a warm, shallow sea, about 520 million years ago. The rock is full of small cups and cones, most of them a few centimetres across, each with a double wall full of holes. They were archaeocyaths ("AR-kee-oh-SIGH-aths"), animals that were probably sponges. Growing together with microbes that also made lime, they built mounds of rock on the sea floor: some of the first big reefs built partly by animals.

Around reefs like these, and on sea floors everywhere, lived animals with hard parts. That is what is new: shells, spines and armour, and eyes too, not in a few kinds of animal but in thousands. A few animals had made shells before (*Bites and shells*). Now hard parts were everywhere, and because hard parts last, the rocks fill with fossils (*Animals, kept*).

Within about twenty million years, fossils turn up of most of the great branches of the animal family alive today: animals with jointed legs, animals with shells in two halves, snails, worms, and the branch with a stiff rod along the back, the one fish belong to. In a few places mud buried animals so fast that their soft parts were kept as well (*Chengjiang*, *Burgess Shale*).

Most of the land lay south of the equator, much of it joined in one great continent, Gondwana (*The map clears*). The sea was warm, and it rose through the stretch. The air held less oxygen than it does now.
Fifty-two million years is nearly four fifths as long as the whole Mammals line.

Geologists call this stretch the Cambrian ("KAM-bree-un"), from Cambria, the name for Wales in medieval Latin, where Adam Sedgwick, an English geologist, studied its rocks. He gave it the name in 1835.
At its end the sea was full of animals. On land, as far as anyone can tell, nothing grew but films of microbes.

references: Françoise Debrenne, "Lower Cambrian Archaeocyatha from the Ajax Mine, Beltana, South Australia," *Bulletin of the British Museum (Natural History), Geology*, 1969. The scene.
Noel James and David Gravestock, "Lower Cambrian shelf and shelf margin buildups, Flinders Ranges, South Australia," *Sedimentology*, 1990. The reefs.
John Paterson, Gregory Edgecombe and Michael Lee, "Trilobite evolutionary rates constrain the duration of the Cambrian explosion," *PNAS*, 2019. The oldest trilobites.
Stephen Jay Gould, *Wonderful Life* (W. W. Norton, 1989). For a parent.

Crowded seas.name: Crowded seas
Crowded seas.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 486.85 ± 1.5 (Green Point, Newfoundland) and 443.1 ± 0.9 (Dob's Linn, Scotland)
Crowded seas.officialName: Ordovician, after the Ordovices, a people of north Wales in Roman times; named by Charles Lapworth in 1879
Crowded seas.knownFrom: shells by the billion in limestone, laid down in warm, shallow seas that covered much of the continents
Crowded seas.insideIt: events *Plants ashore*, *Short, sharp ice* (at the end edge). Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen*.
Crowded seas.picturesWanted: a slab of Cincinnati limestone packed with shells (Cincinnati Museum Center or Commons; licence to check); *Isotelus*, Ohio's state fossil (Cincinnati Museum Center; licence to ask).
Crowded seas.summary: Shallow seas spread over the continents and filled with life, until there were three or four times as many kinds of sea animal as at the start. On land, the oldest signs of plants. It ended in ice.

more.spanLine: From about 487 to 444 million years ago.
paragraphs: In and around Cincinnati, in Ohio, the hillsides and creek beds are made of thin grey layers of limestone and mud, and much of the limestone is nothing but shells. About 450 million years ago this was the floor of a warm, shallow sea, south of the equator, in a belt of storms. The storms heaped the shells into beds.

Pick up a slab and there are shells in two halves, from fingernail to coin size; little stony twigs and crusts that were colonies of tiny animals; stems of sea lilies, animals related to starfish that stood on stalks; and trilobites. One trilobite, *Isotelus* ("eye-so-TEE-lus"), grew longer than a hand. Hunting over the sea floor were animals with long, straight, pointed shells, relatives of the nautilus, the octopus and the squid. The biggest piece of such a shell ever found is three metres long, and it is only part of a shell.
That is what is new: how many kinds of animal there were. In about twenty-five million years the number of kinds of sea animal grew three or four times over. Trilobites came in more shapes than ever.

The seas themselves spread. Sea level stood higher than at almost any other time we know of, perhaps a hundred and fifty metres above today's, and by some estimates more than two hundred, and shallow seas covered much of the continents.

On land, about 470 million years ago, plants left spores in rock in what is now Argentina, the oldest sign of plants on land that most specialists accept (*Plants ashore*). The plants themselves have never been found.
Forty-three million years is about two thirds as long as the Mammals line.

Geologists call this stretch the Ordovician ("or-duh-VISH-un"), after the Ordovices, a people who lived in north Wales when the Romans came. Charles Lapworth, an English geologist, gave it the name in 1879.
At its end, ice spread over what is now North Africa, which then lay near the South Pole, and the seas grew cold. Most kinds of sea animal died out (*Short, sharp ice*).

references: David Harper, "The Ordovician biodiversification: setting an agenda for marine life," *Palaeogeography, Palaeoclimatology, Palaeoecology*, 2006. Three to four times as many families.
Thomas Servais and others, "Understanding the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event (GOBE): influences of paleogeography, paleoclimate, or paleoecology?," *GSA Today*, 2009.
Cole Edwards, Matthew Saltzman, Dana Royer and David Fike, "Oxygenation as a driver of the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event," *Nature Geoscience*, 2017.
David Meyer and Richard Davis, *A Sea Without Fish: Life in the Ordovician Sea of the Cincinnati Region* (Indiana University Press, 2009). For a parent.

Green land.name: Green land
Green land.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 443.1 ± 0.9 (Dob's Linn, Scotland) and 419.62 ± 1.36 (Klonk, Czech Republic)
Green land.officialName: Silurian, after the Silures, a people of south-east Wales in Roman times; named by Roderick Murchison in 1835
Green land.knownFrom: small plants pressed flat in river and shore mud, spores, charcoal, and fossils in sea rock
Green land.insideIt: events *Short, sharp ice* (at the start edge), *Jaws*, *Animals ashore*. Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen*.
Green land.picturesWanted: a *Cooksonia* fossil (Natural History Museum, London, or Commons; licence to check); a drawing of *Cooksonia* at life size (to make).
Green land.summary: After the ice, plants stood up. Along rivers and shores grew green stems a few centimetres tall, with no leaves. Small animals came onto the land. In the sea, fish with jaws spread.

more.spanLine: From about 444 to 419 million years ago.
paragraphs: At Perton, near Stoke Edith, in Herefordshire, close to the border with Wales, there is rock from near the end of this stretch, laid down where rivers ran into the sea. A plant from it is called *Cooksonia* ("cook-SOH-nee-a"), after Isabel Cookson, the Australian botanist who collected it.

*Cooksonia* was a few centimetres tall. It had no leaves and no flowers: only thin green stems that forked, and forked again, with a small round case at the tip of each branch, full of spores. A bank covered in it would have been green, and none of it taller than a finger.

That is what is new: plants that stood up. Plants had been on land for some forty million years already (*Plants ashore*), but as far as anyone knows they lay low and flat, like liverworts. To stand up, a plant needs stiff stems, with pipes inside to carry water up from the ground. Some fossils of *Cooksonia* show such pipes.

The stretch began just after the great ice had shrunk, when most kinds of sea animal had died (*Short, sharp ice*). The seas grew warm again and stood high. Fish with jaws spread through them (*Jaws*), and sea scorpions, some of them about two metres long, hunted in the shallows.
Small animals came onto the land. The oldest one known to have breathed air was like a little millipede, from Stonehaven, in Scotland, though its age is argued (*Animals ashore*).

The tallest living thing on land was not a plant but *Prototaxites* ("pro-toe-tax-EYE-teez"), most likely a fungus: a trunk with no branches. The biggest found, a little younger than this stretch, stood about eight metres tall.
Twenty-five million years is a little over a third as long as the Mammals line.

Geologists call it the Silurian ("sigh-LOOR-ee-un"), after the Silures, a people who lived in south-east Wales when the Romans came. Roderick Murchison, a Scottish geologist, gave it the name in 1835.

references: William Lang, "On the plant-remains from the Downtonian of England and Wales," *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B*, 1937. *Cooksonia* named.

Milan Libertín and others, "Sporophytes of polysporangiate land plants from the early Silurian period may have been photosynthetically autonomous," *Nature Plants*, 2018. The oldest *Cooksonia*, about 432 million.
Ian Glasspool and Robert Gastaldo, "Silurian wildfire proxies and atmospheric oxygen," *Geology*, 2022. The oldest charcoal.
Thomas Halliday, *Otherlands* (Allen Lane, 2022). For a parent.

Fish.name: Fish
Fish.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 419.62 ± 1.36 (Klonk, Czech Republic) and 358.86 ± 0.19 (La Serre, France, a point now under review)
Fish.officialName: Devonian, after Devon, in England; named by Adam Sedgwick and Roderick Murchison in 1839
Fish.knownFrom: whole fish in limestone and red sandstone, fossil forests, footprints, and the daily growth lines of corals
Fish.insideIt: events *Forests*, *Tiktaalik*. Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen*, *Day length* (about 22 hours at 390, from Wells's corals).
Fish.picturesWanted: a Gogo fish freed from its nodule (Western Australian Museum or Museums Victoria; licence to ask); *Materpiscis* with its embryo (Museums Victoria; licence to ask).
Fish.summary: The seas held fish of every shape: fish in armour of bone, sharks, fish with fleshy fins built on bones. On land, plants grew into trees, and forests spread. In a river lived a fish with fins nearly like legs.

more.spanLine: From about 419 to 359 million years ago.
paragraphs: In the Kimberley, in the far north of Western Australia, a line of limestone hills was once a reef in a warm sea, about 380 million years ago. Beside the reef the water was deep and still, with little oxygen. Dead fish sank into it and were sealed in lumps of lime before they could rot. Today, when collectors soak those lumps in weak acid, the same acid that is in vinegar, the fish come out whole, every bone in place.

Many of the Gogo fish were placoderms ("PLAK-o-derms"), fish whose heads and chests were covered in plates of bone, with sharp-edged plates of bone in their jaws. One, named *Materpiscis*, "mother fish", has a young one inside her, still joined by its cord: one of the oldest known animals with backbones to give birth to live young.

That is what is new: fish of every shape. Armoured fish, sharks, fish with thin rays in their fins like most fish today, and fish with fleshy fins built on bones. The biggest of the armoured fish, *Dunkleosteus*, was about three or four metres long.

Fish were not new. Fish with jaws are known from about 439 million years ago (*Jaws*), and fish without jaws from long before. The name marks the time when fish were the most noticed animals, not when they began.

The oldest forest yet found grew where Somerset is now, about 390 million years ago (*Forests*), and by the end of the stretch there were trees with wood and leaves in many places. In rivers lived fish with necks and bony fins (*Tiktaalik*).
A year then had about four hundred days, as fossil corals count them.
Sixty million years is nearly as long as the whole Mammals line.
Geologists call this stretch the Devonian ("di-VOH-nee-un"), after Devon, in England. Adam Sedgwick and Roderick Murchison gave it the name in 1839.
It ended in a long run of dyings. Reefs like the one at Gogo were among the worst hit, and by the end every armoured fish was gone.

references: John Long, Kate Trinajstic, Gavin Young and Tim Senden, "Live birth in the Devonian period," *Nature*, 2008. *Materpiscis*.
Russell Engelman, "A Devonian fish tale: a new method of body length estimation suggests much smaller sizes for *Dunkleosteus terrelli* (Placodermi: Arthrodira)," *Diversity*, 2023.
Lauren Sallan and Michael Coates, "End-Devonian extinction and a bottleneck in the early evolution of modern jawed vertebrates," *PNAS*, 2010.
Neil Shubin, *Your Inner Fish* (Pantheon, 2008). For a parent.

Coal forests.name: Coal forests
Coal forests.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 358.86 ± 0.19 (La Serre, France, under review) and 298.9 ± 0.15 (Aidaralash, Kazakhstan)
Coal forests.officialName: Carboniferous, "coal-bearing", from the Latin *carbo*, coal; named by William Conybeare and William Phillips in 1822. In North America it is split into the Mississippian and the Pennsylvanian.
Coal forests.knownFrom: coal and the plants pressed in it, fossil tree stumps, insects in mudstone
Coal forests.insideIt: events *Land egg*, *Coal*. Plots: *Oxygen* (the high near 305), *Sea level*, *Day length*.
Coal forests.picturesWanted: the *Meganeura* fossil from Commentry (Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle, Paris; licence to ask); a scale-tree trunk with its diamond pattern (Commons; licence to check).
Coal forests.summary: Swamp forests grew along the warm middle of the world, and their dead plants became coal. The air held more oxygen than it does now. Some insects had wings seventy centimetres across, and a millipede grew longer than a person.

more.spanLine: From about 359 to 299 million years ago.
paragraphs: Stand in a coal swamp near the end of this stretch and the trees are like nothing alive. The tallest are scale trees: bare poles thirty metres high or more, a metre or more thick at the base, with a crown of branches only at the very top. Their bark is covered in diamond-shaped scars where leaves once grew. Their nearest relatives alive today are small plants called quillworts.

Over the water flies *Meganeura* ("meg-a-NEW-ra"), its wings about seventy centimetres across. Its fossils come from coal mines at Commentry, in France. It looked like a dragonfly, but it belonged to a group of insects that is now gone, sometimes called griffinflies. On the forest floor lived *Arthropleura*, a millipede that grew to more than two and a half metres long.

That is what is new: forests so wide and so wet that their dead plants piled up faster than they could rot, and were buried, and became coal (*Coal*). The swamps grew in a belt along the equator, where the continents were coming together into one.
The air held more oxygen than it does now: at least a quarter as much again, and perhaps more (*Oxygen*).
Near the South Pole, ice sheets grew and melted many times. Each time the sea fell and rose, so layers of swamp and layers of sea lie stacked one on another.

Animals with backbones walked the land. Clawed footprints about 355 million years old, in Victoria, Australia, may have been made by animals whose eggs could be laid on dry land. By about 315 million years ago, small animals like lizards were trapped in hollow tree stumps in Nova Scotia (*Land egg*).
About 305 million years ago the climate grew drier, and the great swamp forests broke apart into patches.
Sixty million years is nearly as long as the whole Mammals line.
Geologists call this stretch the Carboniferous ("kar-buh-NIF-er-us"), "coal-bearing". William Conybeare and William Phillips, two English geologists, gave it the name in 1822.

references: Sarda Sahney, Michael Benton and Howard Falcon-Lang, "Rainforest collapse triggered Carboniferous tetrapod diversification in Euramerica," *Geology*, 2010.
Benjamin Mills and others, "Evolution of atmospheric O₂ through the Phanerozoic, revisited," *Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences*, 2023.
Matthew Nelsen and others, "Delayed fungal evolution did not cause the Paleozoic peak in coal production," *PNAS*, 2016.
David Beerling, *The Emerald Planet* (Oxford University Press, 2007). For a parent.

One continent.name: One continent
One continent.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 298.9 ± 0.15 (Aidaralash, Kazakhstan) and 251.902 ± 0.024 (Meishan, Zhejiang)
One continent.officialName: Permian, after Perm, an old province of Russia on the western side of the Ural Mountains; named by Roderick Murchison in 1841
One continent.knownFrom: red rock laid down by rivers, desert sand and salt, reefs
One continent.insideIt: events *Dimetrodon* (new, below), *The Great Dying* (at the end edge). Plots: *Oxygen*, *Sea level*.
One continent.picturesWanted: the red beds near Seymour, Texas (Commons; licence to check); a map of Pangaea at 270 million years (our own map, at that year).
One continent.summary: Nearly all the land was joined in one continent, Pangaea, with dry country far from the sea. Most of the largest animals on land were on the same branch of the family as mammals. It ended in the Great Dying.

more.spanLine: From about 299 to 252 million years ago.
paragraphs: In the ranch country around Seymour, in north Texas, the ground is red: old river mud and old soil, stained by rusted iron. About 280 million years ago rivers wound through it to ponds, with ferns by the water and conifers on the drier ground. In the ponds lived a fresh-water shark and *Diplocaulus*, an amphibian with a head shaped like a boomerang. Along the banks walked *Dimetrodon*, three metres long, with a tall sail on its back (*Dimetrodon*).
*Dimetrodon* was not a dinosaur. It died out about forty million years before the oldest dinosaurs yet found. It was not a reptile either. It belonged to the same great branch of animals as mammals.

What is new is one continent. Through the stretch before, the continents had been coming together, and now nearly all the land was joined, from near the South Pole to far into the north, in one great continent, Pangaea ("pan-JEE-a"), Greek for "all the Earth". Its middle was far from any sea. Much of it was dry, with deserts in many places and great rains in their season. The ice near the South Pole melted away early in the stretch.

On land, most of the largest animals were on the mammals' branch: first sail-backs like *Dimetrodon*, and later animals with sabre teeth, and plant-eaters with tusks and beaks. In the south grew forests of a tree called *Glossopteris*. Its fossil leaves, found in Africa, India, South America, Australia and Antarctica, helped show, long afterwards, that those lands had once been joined.
Forty-seven million years is about seven tenths as long as the Mammals line.
Geologists call this stretch the Permian ("PUR-mee-un"), after Perm, an old province of Russia west of the Ural Mountains, where Roderick Murchison studied its rocks. He gave it the name in 1841.
It ended in the Great Dying, when four in five kinds of sea animal died out, probably because of volcanoes in Siberia (*The Great Dying*).

references: Seth Burgess, Samuel Bowring and Shu-zhong Shen, "High-precision timeline for Earth's most severe extinction," *PNAS*, 2014. The end.
Steven Stanley, "Estimates of the magnitudes of major marine mass extinctions in earth history," *PNAS*, 2016. Four in five.
Kirstin Brink and Robert Reisz, "Hidden dental diversity in the oldest terrestrial apex predator *Dimetrodon*," *Nature Communications*, 2014.
Michael Benton, *When Life Nearly Died* (Thames & Hudson, revised 2015). For a parent.

First dinosaurs.name: First dinosaurs
First dinosaurs.spanNote: both edges dated boundaries at points in the rock: 251.902 ± 0.024 (Meishan, Zhejiang) and 201.4 ± 0.2 (Kuhjoch, Austria); the dying that ends it is dated a little earlier, 201.56 (*Triassic ends*)
First dinosaurs.officialName: Triassic, "threefold", for three layers of rock that lie one on another in Germany; named by Friedrich von Alberti in 1834
First dinosaurs.knownFrom: bones and footprints in river and lake beds, red sandstone, salt
First dinosaurs.insideIt: events *The Great Dying* (at the start edge), *Lystrosaurus*, *Dinosaurs*, *Pangaea cracks* and *Triassic ends* (at the end edge). Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen*.
First dinosaurs.picturesWanted: the *Coelophysis* block at the New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science, or the quarry at Ghost Ranch (licence to ask); a *Coelophysis* skeleton (Commons; licence to check).
First dinosaurs.summary: All the land was one hot continent, slowly filling with life after the Great Dying. Dinosaurs appeared about twenty million years in, and stayed few; crocodile relatives were commoner. The oldest turtles and flying reptiles lived then too.

more.spanLine: From about 252 to 201 million years ago.
paragraphs: At Ghost Ranch, in northern New Mexico, there is a quarry where in 1947 a museum team found a bed of dinosaur bones, skeleton lying on skeleton: hundreds of them, perhaps more than a thousand animals. All are *Coelophysis* ("see-lo-FY-sis"), a slender hunter up to three metres long, most of it neck and tail, about as heavy as a middle-sized dog. How so many died together is argued; a flood is the leading guess. They lived late in this stretch, perhaps 205 million years ago.

They were late. For nearly the first twenty million years of this stretch there were no dinosaurs at all (*Dinosaurs*). Even after the dinosaurs appeared, they were few. The crocodile side of the reptile family was commoner and came in more shapes: long-snouted fish-eaters, armoured plant-eaters, big hunters that walked upright.
What is new is a crowd of new kinds of animal, and many of their families are still alive: the oldest turtles, the oldest flying reptiles, small animals very close to the mammals, and the dinosaurs.

The stretch began in an emptied world, just after the Great Dying, when one plant-eater, *Lystrosaurus*, was by far the commonest animal in many places (*Lystrosaurus*). All the land was one continent, Pangaea. Its middle was hot and dry, and there was no ice at either pole. About 233 million years ago, rain fell hard, on and off, for about two million years.
Fifty-one million years is more than a quarter of the Dinosaurs line, and about three quarters as long as the Mammals line.

Geologists call this stretch the Triassic ("try-ASS-ik"), "threefold", for three layers of rock that lie one on another in Germany: a coloured sandstone, a limestone full of shells, and coloured clays. Friedrich von Alberti, a German geologist, gave it the name in 1834.

It ended about 201 million years ago, when Pangaea began to crack and lava poured out along the cracks (*Pangaea cracks*). The big relatives of crocodiles died. The dinosaurs lived on (*Triassic ends*).

references: Jacopo Dal Corso and others, "Extinction and dawn of the modern world in the Carnian (Late Triassic)," *Science Advances*, 2020. The rains.

Larry Rinehart and others, "The paleobiology of *Coelophysis bauri* (Cope) from the Upper Triassic (Apachean) Whitaker quarry, New Mexico, with detailed analysis of a single quarry block," *New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science Bulletin*, 2009.
Stephen Brusatte, Michael Benton, Marcello Ruta and Graeme Lloyd, "Superiority, competition, and opportunism in the evolutionary radiation of dinosaurs," *Science*, 2008. The crocodile side first.
Nicholas Fraser, *Dawn of the Dinosaurs: Life in the Triassic* (Indiana University Press, 2006). For a parent.

Giants.name: Giants
Giants.spanNote: the start a dated boundary at a point in the rock, 201.4 ± 0.2 (Kuhjoch, Austria); the end a boundary fixed by agreement, 143.1 ± 0.6, with no point in the rock yet. 143 replaces 145 (Michael, 10 Oct): the chart moved it in v2024/12.
Giants.officialName: Jurassic, after the Jura Mountains, on the border of France and Switzerland; Alexander von Humboldt called their limestone "Jura limestone" in 1799, and Alexandre Brongniart made it the name of a stretch of time in 1829
Giants.knownFrom: bone beds in old river sand, footprints, sea rock full of ammonites, and the oldest parts of the ocean floor
Giants.insideIt: events *Pangaea cracks* and *Triassic ends* (at the start edge), *Big footprints* (new, below), *Archaeopteryx*. Plots: *Sea level*, *Oxygen*.
Giants.picturesWanted: the wall of bones in the Quarry Exhibit Hall, Dinosaur National Monument (National Park Service, public domain; to confirm); a map of Pangaea splitting at 170 million years (our own map, at that year).
Giants.summary: Dinosaurs ruled the land, and the long-necked plant-eaters grew into some of the largest animals that ever walked. Pangaea split, and a narrow Atlantic opened. *Archaeopteryx* flew on feathered wings.

more.spanLine: From about 201 to 143 million years ago.
paragraphs: At Dinosaur National Monument, in Utah, a hall has been built against a wall of tilted sandstone. In the wall are about fifteen hundred dinosaur bones, left where they lie: backbones, ribs, leg bones, a skull here and there. About 150 million years ago this was a river. Animals died in dry years, and floods washed their bones onto a sandbar and buried them.

Earl Douglass, of the Carnegie Museum, found the first of them in 1909: eight bones of a tail, sticking out of the rock. Most of the bones are from long-necked plant-eaters, *Apatosaurus*, *Diplodocus* and *Camarasaurus*. With them are *Stegosaurus*, with plates along its back, and *Allosaurus*, a hunter.

That is what is new: giants. The long-necked dinosaurs, called sauropods ("SORE-o-pods"), grew longer and heavier than any land animal before them. Some in this stretch were more than twenty-five metres long and weighed as much as several elephants. The very largest came later (*Flowers*).

The dinosaurs took over the land at the start, after a dying that took many of their rivals (*Triassic ends*). In eastern North America, footprints of big meat-eating dinosaurs appear in the rock within ten thousand years (*Big footprints*).

Pangaea came apart. North America pulled away from Africa, and between them a narrow Atlantic Ocean opened. The world was warm, with no ice at the poles. Late in the stretch, on islands in a warm sea where Bavaria is now, lived *Archaeopteryx*, an animal with feathered wings, teeth and a long bony tail (*Archaeopteryx*).
Fifty-eight million years is nearly a third of the Dinosaurs line.

Geologists call this stretch the Jurassic ("joo-RASS-ik"), after the Jura Mountains, on the border of France and Switzerland. Alexander von Humboldt named the limestone of the Jura in 1799, and Alexandre Brongniart, a French geologist, made it the name of a stretch of time in 1829.
Where this stretch ends has not yet been tied to a layer of rock anywhere in the world.

references: National Park Service, "Quarry Exhibit Hall," Dinosaur National Monument (nps.gov/dino). About 1,500 bones.
Kim Cohen, David Harper, Philip Gibbard and Nicholas Car, "The ICS International Chronostratigraphic Chart this decade," *Episodes*, 2025. The new end date.
Paul Olsen and others, "Ascent of dinosaurs linked to an iridium anomaly at the Triassic-Jurassic boundary," *Science*, 2002.
John Foster, *Jurassic West: The Dinosaurs of the Morrison Formation and Their World* (Indiana University Press, second edition 2020). For a parent.

Flowers.summary: A warm world, with seas high over the land, laying down chalk. Flowering plants appeared and spread, until by the end they were the most varied plants in much of the world. *Tyrannosaurus* lived at the very end.

more.spanLine: From about 143 to 66 million years ago.
paragraphs: The White Cliffs of Dover stand more than a hundred metres over the sea between England and France. They are chalk, and chalk under a microscope is mostly tiny plates of lime, each a few thousandths of a millimetre across. The plates were the armour of single-celled algae called coccolithophores ("cock-o-LITH-o-fores"). When the algae died, their plates sank, and settled on the sea floor, about a centimetre every thousand years, until the chalk was hundreds of metres thick. The cliffs east of Dover are about 94 to 86 million years old.

For the sea floor to be where Dover is, the sea had to be high. At their highest, shallow seas covered about a third of today's land, and one cut North America in two. Between about 90 and 80 million years ago, guesses for the height of the sea run from about fifty metres above today's to more than two hundred (*Sea level*). The world was warm, with no large ice sheets for most of the stretch.

What is new is flowers. Pollen of flowering plants goes back about 135 million years. Among the oldest whole flowering plants yet found are water plants with no petals, about 125 million years old (*Oldest flowers*). By the end of the stretch, flowering plants were the most varied plants in much of the world, though conifers and ferns still made up much of many forests.

The dinosaurs went on, and some grew larger than ever. *Argentinosaurus*, from about 95 million years ago, was perhaps thirty-five metres long, among the largest animals ever to walk. At the very end lived *Tyrannosaurus* and *Triceratops*.
Seventy-seven million years is longer than the whole Mammals line.

Geologists call this stretch the Cretaceous ("kri-TAY-shus"), "chalky", from *creta*, the Latin word for chalk. Jean-Baptiste d'Omalius d'Halloy, a Belgian geologist, gave it the name in 1822, for the chalk around Paris.
It ended about 66 million years ago, when an asteroid about ten kilometres across hit what is now Yucatán, in Mexico (*The asteroid*).

references: Kenneth Miller and others, "The Phanerozoic record of global sea-level change," *Science*, 2005.
Bernard Gomez and others, "*Montsechia*, an ancient aquatic angiosperm," *PNAS*, 2015.
Scott Wing and Lisa Boucher, "Ecological aspects of the Cretaceous flowering plant radiation," *Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences*, 1998. Most varied, not most of the forest.
Thomas Henry Huxley, "On a Piece of Chalk" (1868; free online). For a parent.
